title: Orbital Cavernous Hemangioma: The Clinical Mastery Guide
summary: The most common benign primary orbital neoplasm in adults. This slow-growing, encapsulated vascular lesion is characterized by its distinct clinical, imaging, and histopathological features, requiring precise diagnostic differentiation from other orbital pathologies.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
content: Definition: A benign, low-flow, encapsulated vascular malformation of the orbit.
Incidence: Accounts for ~5-10% of all orbital tumors.
Demographics: Typically presents in the 3rd to 5th decade of life.
Gender: Female-to-male ratio of 2:1, suggesting potential hormonal influence (progesterone/estrogen receptors found).
Location: Most commonly found within the intraconal space (muscle cone), lateral to the optic nerve.

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Histology
sections.content: Not a true neoplasm, but a hamartoma composed of large, blood-filled, endothelium-lined spaces separated by fibrous septa. Lacks significant feeding arteries or draining veins, explaining its characteristic 'slow-flow' imaging profile.

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Insidious, painless, progressive proptosis.
Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) loss due to optic nerve compression or induced hyperopia (choroidal compression).
Diplopia from restriction of extraocular motility.
Retinochoroidal folds (focal retinal pigment epithelium changes).

rows: Enhances more intensely on delayed MRI
Associated with URI, cystic, prone to hemorrhage

sections.title: Imaging Characteristics (Gold Standard)
content: CT Scan: Well-circumscribed, round/oval, hyperdense lesion. May show calcification (phleboliths).
MRI T1: Isointense to extraocular muscles.
MRI T2: Hyperintense (bright) with internal septations.
Contrast Dynamics: Initial patchy, centripetal enhancement followed by progressive filling (a hallmark sign).

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Observation for asymptomatic, small, stable lesions.
Step 2: Indications for surgery: Progressive vision loss, diplopia, significant proptosis, or cosmetic deformity.
Step 3: Surgical approach: Lateral orbitotomy (Krönlein approach) is the gold standard for intraconal lesions.
Step 4: Post-operative monitoring: Monitor for optic nerve edema or motility disturbances.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Sudden, painful vision loss (suggests intralesional hemorrhage).
Rapid expansion (suggests misdiagnosis as malignant lesion).
Signs of Optic Neuropathy (APD, color desaturation).
Inability to close eyelids leading to exposure keratopathy.

content.explanation: Slow-growing (painless), Stable (encapsulated), Sequential (progressive filling on imaging).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Most common orbital tumor in adults.
If you see high-flow on Doppler, reconsider the diagnosis (consider AV malformation).
Surgical removal is usually curative with low recurrence risk.
Always evaluate for hyperopia due to globe compression.
